title: Reservation Allocator Dashboard — early wires
body:
Purpose
A compact set of early wireframes and groomed backlog items for a "Reservation Allocator" view in the Dedicated Capacity Console. Focus: let platform & product teams create, inspect, and modify GPU pool reservations, manage burst credits, and reason about autoscaling impacts before committing reserved spend. This doc captures UX goals, proposed components, two primary flows, and a prioritized grooming list with acceptance criteria and open questions.

High-level goals (what success looks like)
- Make reservations visible and discoverable (who reserved what, when it will start/end, linked routes).
- Surface cost and latency trade-offs up-front (estimated $/hour, expected median latency per workload class).
- Prevent overlapping/conflicting reservations via visual conflict detection and soft resolution suggestions.
- Give teams clear controls for bursts: credit bank, per-reservation burst limits, and automatic replenishment policies.
- Make autoscaling policy effects immediate and inspectable (simulate a 5–10 minute horizon).

Design constraints & assumptions
- Dedicated customers may have multi-tenant pools across teams. Reservations are bound to a pool and optionally to a route/tag.
- Backward-compatible with existing pool list page; this is an additional detailed view linked from pools and billing pages.
- Role-based permissions: only pool admins can create/modify reservations; devs can request/attach but require approval.

Primary components (wireframe-level)
1) Top summary bar: pool selector, active reservation count, aggregate capacity reserved vs available (in vGPU units), live utilization sparkline (1h/24h). Quick actions: "New Reservation", "Request Credits", "Simulate Policy".

2) Timeline canvas: horizontal timeline showing existing reservations as blocks, color-coded by team/route, with capacity band overlays (total GPUs vs reserved vs scheduled autoscale). Hover reveals reservation metadata (owner, start/end, vGPU count, burst cap, linked routes, cost estimate).

3) Reservation inspector panel (right rail): when a block is clicked, slide-over panel shows editable fields: name, owner, start/end, recurrence, pool selector, vGPU count, burst-policy (manual/auto), preemption policy (none/soft/hard), linked routes, approval status, notes. Action buttons: Save draft, Submit (for approval), Cancel.

4) Burst credits bank modal: shows pool-level bank and per-reservation allocations. UI shows current bank balance, projected consumption under current traffic percentile (p50/p95), and controls to top-up (charge to team account) or set auto-replenish (threshold + refill amount).

5) Autoscaling scenario simulator: small interactive widget that lets users toggle scale out aggressiveness, cold-start penalty, and P99 latency threshold to see how many GPUs would be needed during a simulated 10-minute spike. Shows cost delta for changes and suggested reservation increase.

6) Conflicts & suggestions strip: if a new or edited reservation overlaps and would oversubscribe the pool for any minute in the timeline, show a red conflict badge and suggestions: shift start by X minutes, reduce vGPU count, borrow from burst bank, or request additional compute (link to capacity cart).

Main flows (stepwise)
Flow A — Create a reservation (pool admin):
1. Click "New Reservation" from top bar (or from a pool row).
2. Modal opens with 4 columns: Basic (name, owner, team), Timing (start/end, recurrence presets), Capacity (vGPU count, profile), Policy (burst cap, preemption policy, approval).
3. Enter values; autoscaling simulator warns if profile conflicts with autoscale policy (e.g., reserving more than max_scale).
4. Click "Preview timeline" — modal collapses to show proposed block superimposed on timeline with live conflict check.
5. If no conflict, click "Save & Submit" — triggers approval flow if owner not pool admin.
6. System enqueues reservation; approval notifications to approvers and a pending state visible on timeline.

Acceptance criteria for Flow A:
- Preview shows exact capacity usage per-minute for the reservation window.
- Conflict detection flags any minute where total requested > physical capacity.
- Submitting non-admin creates a request with metadata and sends a notification to approvers (Jira task created).

Flow B — Temporarily burst beyond reservation (team dev):
1. Dev opens Reservation Allocator and finds their reservation block.
2. Click "Request burst" -> Burst modal opens showing bank balance and forecasted consumption.
3. Select burst amount, choose auto-replenish checkbox (optional), add justification.
4. If within bank limit and auto-approve policy exists, funds allocated immediately and timeline updates. Otherwise, request enters approval queue.

Key grooming/backlog items (prioritized)
P0
- Minute-level timeline rendering with efficient tiling (perf): implement virtualized canvas and pre-aggregate usage per minute. (AC: <200ms render for 10k events)
- Conflict detection engine integrated with UI: run fast check for any minute overcommit. (AC: detect conflicts within 1s of change)
- Reservation create/preview modal + approval hook. (AC: create request with metadata saved to backend)

P1
- Burst credits UI + bank model + top-up flow. (AC: show bank, allow top-up via billing flow stub)
- Autoscaling simulator widget integrated with cost calc. (AC: show delta cost and suggested reservation)
- Editable preemption policy and visible fallbacks (route reroute to fallback model).

P2
- Conflict resolution suggestions with click-to-apply adjustments (shift/rescale/borrow).
- Recurring reservations UX and templates (daily/weekly business-hours presets).
- Audit trail & change history for each reservation.

Edge cases & notes
- Extremely short reservations (< 2 minutes) should be disallowed (too noisy) unless flagged as "ephemeral dev test".
- Reservations spanning maintenance windows should surface potential interruptions and allow marking "tolerate preemption for maintenance".
- If multiple teams share pool and approvals cross org boundaries, make approver roster visible on reservation summary.

Open questions for PM/Infra
- Approval model: should auto-approve be on a per-pool basis (admins) or per-team budget?
- Billing granularity: do we bill reservations by minute or by block? (affects cost estimate UI)
- How are burst credits funded? central pool or charged to team budgets?
- What is the canonical source of truth for capacity (scheduler vs billing vs console)? Single API or eventual consistency?

Micro-interaction details to capture for handoff
- On timeline hover, show 2-line tooltip: "Reservation name • owner • vGPU count • cost/hour" and a small link to open inspector. Tooltip should remain if cursor moves within tooltip.
- Drag-to-shift reservation: allow horizontal drag to move start/end; on-drop run conflict check and show green/yellow/red indicator. If red, show suggested small shifts with a confirmation popover.
- Undo stack for edits within 60s of save (soft undo).

Notes for visual design and accessibility
- Color palette: use team colors but ensure reservations by same team use shades with clear outline for contrast. Provide pattern + color for colorblind-friendly view.
- Keyboard accessibility: allow reservation selection with arrow keys, open inspector with Enter, quick-create with Ctrl+N.

Next steps (who does what)
- Jonah: produce high-fidelity mockups for timeline + inspector (due 2024-10-09).
- Asha: prototype minute-level canvas performance strategy with infra (due 2024-10-04).
- Liam: spec API contract for conflict detection and preview (JIRA-INF-8427).
- Priya: define approval workflows and billing interactions; sync with finance.

Appendix: short copy snippets for UI
- "New reservation" modal header: Create reservation for <pool>
- Timeline conflict toast: "Reservation conflicts with existing allocation from 10:12 to 10:32 — reduce vGPU or pick a different window."
- Burst modal CTA: "Request burst — allocate from pool bank (pending approval)"

This is intentionally an early-stage working doc — expect many iterations. Add notes in the comment thread or link UX mocks back to the GitHub PR above.
